title: DeepSeek's rate-limiting isn't about money—it's falling behind the US on computing power
dek: DeepSeek's throttling of consumer service is not about saving money—it's because domestic chips lag far behind overseas leaders in both quantity and generation, so model companies would rather pull chips back for training than serve ordinary users.
why: Information-dense: breaks down the bottleneck into data, talent, and computing power, explaining each layer thoroughly—essential listening for anyone who wants to understand the true state of domestic AI.
who: Entrepreneurs and investors tracking China's AI models and computing independence; AI professionals trying to understand why DeepSeek throttles.
skip: The opening complaints about DeepSeek's specific rate-limiting rules have low information density; jump straight to the analysis of computing-power generational gaps.

points.h: Bytedance's abundance stems from early, aggressive purchasing
points.body: The host notes Bytedance has about one million GPUs, with 10,000 new H200s arriving in August 2025. This abundance explains why Bytedance's Doubao (豆包) model avoids DeepSeek-style user throttling—not a technical choice, but inventory depth.

points.h: Your chat data is worthless to model makers
points.body: Xiaobai explains that model training requires data cleaning and diversity; ordinary chat data introduces strange speech patterns requiring costly alignment fixes. Role-playing scenarios have proven commercially dead. What model makers actually want is agentic data—coding-agent execution traces that directly improve AGI capabilities. Chat services are pure cost, not value.

points.h: China's leading chips are over two years behind the US
points.body: Timeline: Nvidia's main chips 2022-2024 were H100 to H800, still powering most Chinese data centers (plus the crippled H20). By 2025, overseas players run B200, GB200, B300 generation. Beyond generation gaps, scale matters: China's three largest companies combined have hundreds of thousands of chips; xAI alone has 780,000 running and nearly 600,000 more on order—totaling well over one million, with newer architectures.

points.h: Chip orchestration was once scarcer than chips themselves
points.body: Xiaobai argues model training bottlenecks were never just data and talent—they were AI infra teams' ability to schedule compute. A million chips distributed badly equals nothing. This explains why AI infra talent commanded premium pay: not chip shortage alone, but no one could truly optimize the cluster.

points.h: Model training still needs humans—AI cannot yet replace the engineer
points.body: Xiaobai distinguishes: AI excels at translating inference approaches from CUDA to Huawei or Alibaba architectures—brute force works. But real model training is rife with novel optimizations and mysterious infra errors that AI struggles to handle. If engineers are replaced and that layer breaks, deeper optimization demands will find no one to meet them.

points.h: China's latest models were trained overseas on the newest chips
points.body: Overseas labs fingerprinted models and found DeepSeek V3.2, Kimi K2, K2 Pro trained on B300/B200—meaning training happened on overseas cloud. As foreign data centers tighten remote-compute restrictions for China, this workaround is being shut down.

points.h: Huawei's 910C reaches half the performance of Nvidia's cards
points.body: Twitter reports show Huawei's 910C achieves H20-level performance at roughly half. Not cutting-edge, but adequate for inference—freeing Nvidia chips for training. This is considered the realistic interim solution.

points.h: Domestic chips lack ecosystem, not engineering
points.body: Xiaobai cites Google Colab: newcomers get free chips to learn on—critical for developing AI talent. Domestic chips lack this. Core reason: insufficient quantity—major companies hoard them, leaving nothing for personal developers. Supply will naturally drive ecosystem building.

quotes.text: Model makers don't want your chat data at all. First, it's trivial to generate. Second, your chat data is fundamentally dirty.
The gap in computing power is enormous. When facing that, people naturally wonder: why must I use my best chips to serve you?
And this is what worries them—if the goal is AGI, they can keep advancing. But if people only provide service at the current stage, there's definitely a limit.
Nothing here is permanent. It's really a test of wisdom and patience.
